title: SECAM: African Church Poised to Shape the Future of Synodality, SECAM President Says
desc:
By: Bezawit Assefa
The President of the Symposium of Episcopal Conferences of Africa and Madagascar (SECAM) has called on Church leaders across Africa to embrace a deeper commitment to synodality, emphasizing communion, participation, and mission as the Church enters a new phase in its journey.
Speaking during his opening address at the continental gathering hosted by the Catholic Bishops' Conference of Ethiopia (CBCE), His Eminence Fridolin Cardinal Ambongo Besungu of Kinshasa in the Democratic Republic of Congo expressed gratitude to the Ethiopian Church for welcoming participants and extended special appreciation to His Eminence Berhaneyesus Demerew Cardinal Souraphiel, President of CBCE, for the hospitality offered to delegates.
Highlighting the significance of the meeting, he stated that the Church is moving into a new stage of becoming a more synodal Church, one that is rooted in listening, shared responsibility, and missionary engagement. He noted that the SECAM Secretariat has been closely accompanying and evaluating the synodal process throughout the continent and has observed a strong commitment among African Churches to walk this path with humility and openness.
The President also reflected on the many challenges facing both the Church and wider society in Africa. He cited poverty, armed conflicts, forced migration, and inadequate formation in synodality as major concerns. In addition, he acknowledged the various pastoral and social difficulties encountered by local communities across the continent.
Despite these challenges, he encouraged participants to approach the seminar in a spirit of discernment. He urged them to pray, listen attentively, engage in meaningful dialogue, and reflect on emerging realities while evaluating pastoral priorities in the light of the Gospel and the needs of God's people.
Describing the gathering as only the beginning of a longer journey, the President stressed that the implementation of the Synod requires ongoing discernment at every level of Church life, from local communities and dioceses to continental structures and the universal Church. He affirmed Africa's desire to make a meaningful contribution to the global synodal process by sharing the continent's experiences, challenges, and hopes.
He further encouraged all participants to remain open to the guidance of the Holy Spirit and to take an active role in shaping the future of the Church through the synodal process.
Expressing hope for the outcomes of the seminar, the SECAM President said the gathering should help strengthen relationships among the Churches of Africa, deepen communion, and reinforce the Church's evangelizing mission throughout the continent and beyond.
May this seminar strengthen and deepen our relationships as we walk together in faith, listening to the Holy Spirit and contributing to the future of the Church in Africa and the universal Church, he said.
He concluded by urging participants to remain attentive to God's guidance throughout their discussions.
Let us listen attentively, not only to one another but, above all, to the voice of the Holy Spirit, he said, expressing hope that the seminar would strengthen communion among the Churches of Africa, deepen their shared responsibility for evangelization, and renew their commitment to becoming an ever more synodal and missionary Church.

title: SECAM: “Synodality Requires Continual Conversion,” Bishop Lucio Tells Church Leaders
desc:
By: Bezawit Assefa
Bishop Lucio Andrice Muandula, Bishop Responsible for the Continental Synodal Journey, presented the roadmap for the implementation of the Synod across the Church, outlining a four-stage process that will culminate in an Ecclesial Assembly in October 2028.
Addressing participants during the continental gathering in Addis-Ababa, Bishop Lucio reflected on the Church's path forward following the approval of the Synod's Final Document in 2024. He emphasized that the Church has entered a new phase in its synodal journey, focused on deepening communion, participation, and mission.
Following the approval of the Final Document in 2024, our Church is on a new path, he said, explaining that the implementation phase is not intended to create a new ecclesial calendar or introduce additional structures. Rather, its purpose to renew and transform the ordinary life of the Church through the practice of synodality.
Bishop Lucio explained that the assemblies scheduled between now and 2028 will serve as moments of discernment, reflection, and synthesis. These gatherings will help the Church evaluate the fruits of the synodal journey and listen attentively to the guidance of the Holy Spirit.
Describing synodal evaluation as a process of spiritual discernment, he invited participants to reflect on fundamental questions: where the presence of the Holy Spirit is being manifested, what fruits have emerged from the process so far, and where the Risen Lord is calling the Church today. He also encouraged delegates to assess the concrete steps already taken and identify new opportunities opening before the Church.
Highlighting the need for ongoing renewal, Bishop Lucio stressed that synodality requires continual conversion and outlined the four stages that will guide the implementation process.
The first stage will focus on Diocesan Assemblies, which are expected to be convened in every diocese by the first half of 2027. During this phase, local Churches will evaluate their synodal experience and prepare narrative reports documenting their journey, challenges, achievements, and lessons learned.
The second stage will involve National and Episcopal Conference Discernment. Bishops' Conferences, working alongside theologians and other experts, will review diocesan reports, identify emerging pastoral priorities, and assess key challenges and opportunities highlighted at the local level.
The third stage will consist of Continental Assemblies, bringing together Episcopal Conferences and regional representatives. These assemblies will examine findings from across the continent, identify common pastoral priorities, and develop shared orientations for the Church. The continental phase will also foster dialogue with other regions of the world and collaboration with the Holy See.
The process will reach its fourth stage with the Ecclesial Assembly of October 2028, which will include the active participation of the People of God. The fruits gathered through four years of listening, discernment, and implementation will be presented to the Holy Father as part of the Church's ongoing synodal journey.
In his concluding remarks, Bishop Lucio emphasized that the 2028 Assembly should not be viewed merely as the end of a process or a celebratory event. Instead, he said, it will mark the beginning of a renewed chapter in the life and mission of the Church.
The conclusion in 2028 is not merely a celebration; it is the beginning of a renewed journey for the Church as we continue to grow in communion, participation, and mission, Bishop Lucio said.
His presentation underscored the Church's commitment to ensuring that synodality becomes an integral part of its everyday life, guiding pastoral action and strengthening participation at every level of the Church.
